subject: Chemistry
title: Chemical Thermodynamics
summary: The system is what we study; the surroundings are everything else. An open system exchanges energy and matter, a closed one only energy, an isolated one neither. State functions (U, H, S, G, p, V, T) depend only on the initial and final states; heat and work are path functions.

The first law is energy conservation: ΔU = q + w (chemistry sign convention: work done ON the system and heat given TO the system are positive). Heat at constant volume = ΔU; heat at constant pressure = ΔH.

Enthalpy is additive: by Hess's law the ΔH of any reaction can be found by adding and subtracting other reactions. Formation, combustion, bond, atomisation and phase change enthalpies all link up this way.
Second law: every spontaneous process increases the entropy of the universe (ΔS_total > 0). For the system one number is enough — Gibbs energy: at constant T and p, ΔG < 0 means spontaneous.
ΔG° = −RT ln K links standard Gibbs energy and the equilibrium constant. Negative ΔG° ⇒ K > 1 (products favoured).

formulas.name: First law
formulas.note: Chemistry: work on the system +w, work by the system −w. Physics books use the opposite convention.

formulas.name: Work of expansion (irreversible)
formulas.when: Expansion against a constant external pressure.

formulas.name: Enthalpy
formulas.formula: H = U + pV;   ΔH = ΔU + Δn_g RT
formulas.mistake: Δn_g = moles of gaseous products − moles of gaseous reactants; don't count solids/liquids.

formulas.name: Heat at constant V and p
formulas.when: A bomb calorimeter (constant V) gives ΔU; a coffee-cup calorimeter (constant p) gives ΔH.

formulas.name: Heat capacity
formulas.formula: q = C ΔT = n C_m ΔT;   C_p − C_V = R (ideal gas, molar);   monoatomic: C_V = 3R/2, C_p = 5R/2
formulas.note: Specific heat (per gram) and molar heat capacity (per mole) are different.

formulas.name: Adiabatic process
formulas.formula: q = 0 ⇒ ΔU = w;   reversible ideal gas: TV^{γ−1} = constant,  pV^γ = constant
formulas.note: In reversible adiabatic expansion the gas cools (it does work from its own internal energy). Free expansion of an ideal gas: ΔT = 0.

formulas.name: Hess's law
formulas.formula: ΔH (overall) = ΔH₁ + ΔH₂ + …   (reverse a reaction → reverse the sign of ΔH;  ×n → ΔH × n)
formulas.when: ΔH of reactions that can't be measured directly.

formulas.name: From enthalpies of formation
formulas.formula: Δ_rH° = Σ Δ_fH°(products) − Σ Δ_fH°(reactants);   Δ_fH° of an element in its standard state = 0
formulas.mistake: Don't forget to multiply by the coefficients.

formulas.name: From bond enthalpies
formulas.formula: Δ_rH = Σ BE(reactants, bonds broken) − Σ BE(products, bonds formed)
formulas.note: Here it is reactants − products (opposite of the formation formula).

formulas.name: Types of enthalpy
formulas.formula: Combustion (1 mol + O₂), atomisation (1 mol → gaseous atoms), sublimation = fusion + vaporisation, ionisation, hydration (gaseous ion → aq), solution = lattice + hydration, neutralisation (strong acid + strong base ≈ −57.1 kJ/mol)
formulas.note: With a weak acid/base neutralisation is less exothermic (energy is used for ionisation).

formulas.name: Entropy change
formulas.formula: ΔS = q_rev / T;   phase change: ΔS = ΔH_trans / T_trans;   ideal gas isothermal: ΔS = 2.303 nR log(V₂/V₁)

formulas.name: Gibbs energy
formulas.formula: G = H − TS;   ΔG = ΔH − TΔS;   ΔG = −T ΔS_total
formulas.when: Spontaneity at constant T and p.

formulas.name: Sign table (ΔH, ΔS)
formulas.formula: (−, +): always spontaneous.  (+, −): never.  (−, −): at low T.  (+, +): at high T.   Switch temperature T = ΔH/ΔS
formulas.when: At what temperature a reaction will go.
formulas.note: Convert ΔS from J to kJ before combining it with ΔH.

formulas.name: ΔG° and equilibrium constant
formulas.formula: ΔG° = −RT ln K = −2.303 RT log K;   ΔG = ΔG° + RT ln Q
formulas.note: R = 8.314 J/(K·mol) — keep ΔG° in J.

examples.title: Work against external pressure
examples.problem: A gas expands from 2 L to 10 L against a constant external pressure of 1 atm. Work?
examples.solution: w = −p_ext ΔV = −1 × 8 = −8 L·atm = −8 × 101.3 J ≈ −810 J. Negative: the system did work.

examples.title: Reversible isothermal expansion
examples.problem: 1 mol of ideal gas expands reversibly from 10 L to 20 L at 300 K. w, q, ΔU?

examples.title: ΔU from ΔH
examples.problem: N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) → 2NH₃(g), ΔH = −92.4 kJ at 298 K. ΔU?

examples.title: Hess's law: formation of CO
examples.problem: C + O₂ → CO₂, ΔH = −393.5 kJ;  CO + ½O₂ → CO₂, ΔH = −283.0 kJ. ΔH for C + ½O₂ → CO?

examples.title: Combustion from formation enthalpies
examples.problem: Δ_fH°: CH₄ −74.8, CO₂ −393.5, H₂O(l) −285.8 kJ/mol. Δ_cH° for CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O(l)?

examples.title: ΔH from bond enthalpies
examples.problem: H–H 436, Cl–Cl 242, H–Cl 431 kJ/mol. ΔH for H₂ + Cl₂ → 2HCl?

examples.title: At what temperature is it spontaneous?
examples.problem: CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂: ΔH = +179 kJ/mol, ΔS = +160 J/(K·mol). When spontaneous?
examples.solution: (+, +) ⇒ at high T. T = ΔH/ΔS = 179000/160 ≈ 1119 K and above.

topics.title: System, surroundings and boundary
topics.explain: Open (open boiling kettle): matter + energy exchange. Closed (sealed container): only energy. Isolated (ideal thermos): neither. Universe = system + surroundings.

topics.title: Extensive vs intensive properties
topics.explain: Extensive properties depend on amount: mass, volume, U, H, S, G, heat capacity. Intensive ones don't: T, p, density, molar quantities, specific heat. The ratio of two extensive properties is intensive (density = m/V).

topics.title: State functions vs path functions
topics.explain: State functions depend only on initial and final states (U, H, S, G, p, V, T) — zero change over a cycle. Path functions depend on the route (q, w). But q + w = ΔU is a state function.

topics.title: Processes
topics.explain: Isothermal (constant T), isobaric (constant p), isochoric (constant V), adiabatic (q = 0), cyclic (returns to start: ΔU = 0). Reversible: equilibrium at every step, infinitely slow; irreversible: real, fast processes.

topics.title: Internal energy vs enthalpy
topics.explain: U = total energy of the molecules. H = U + pV, the heat supplied at constant pressure. For solids and liquids ΔH ≈ ΔU; for gases they differ by Δn_g RT.

topics.title: Calorimetry
topics.explain: A bomb calorimeter (sealed, constant V) measures ΔU — used for combustion. A coffee-cup calorimeter (open, constant p) measures ΔH.

topics.title: Standard state and formation
topics.explain: Standard state: 1 bar, given T (usually 298 K), most stable form (C graphite, O₂ gas, Br₂ liquid). Δ_fH° of an element in its standard state is 0. Diamond and O₃ do not have zero Δ_fH°.

topics.title: Lattice and hydration enthalpy
topics.explain: Dissolving an ionic solid = breaking the lattice (+, endothermic) + hydrating the ions (−, exothermic). Δ_solH = lattice + hydration. If hydration is larger, dissolving is exothermic.

topics.title: Meaning of spontaneity
topics.explain: Spontaneous = can happen on its own without outside help (not necessarily fast — e.g. diamond → graphite). ΔH alone does not decide it (melting ice is endothermic yet spontaneous above 0 °C); entropy must also be considered.

topics.title: Feel for entropy
topics.explain: Gas > liquid > solid. Raising temperature, increasing moles of gas, dissolving and expanding all increase entropy. Third law: a perfect crystal has zero entropy at 0 K.

topics.title: ΔG, K and Q
topics.explain: ΔG° < 0 ⇒ K > 1; ΔG° > 0 ⇒ K < 1. At any instant the reaction moves forward or back according to ΔG = ΔG° + RT ln Q; at equilibrium ΔG = 0 and Q = K.
